title: Statements that are true or false
objectives: Tell a statement from a question or an opinion, and decide whether it is true.

screens.title: Right or wrong
screens.prose: Here are eight sentences. Some of them could be marked right or wrong, like a sum in a test. Others cannot be marked at all.

rows: The FTSE 100 is the best index
Every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes

screens.question: Tap every sentence that has to be either true or false.

hints.text: For each sentence, ask: could someone check it and say right or wrong?
A question, an order and a matter of taste cannot be marked.
Rows 1, 3, 6 and 8 each claim something definite. Row 7 depends on what $x$ is.

feedback.correct: Four sentences: 1, 3, 6 and 8. Each one is either true or false.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep a sentence only if it must be either true or false.

byKey.dropped-false: You left out row 3 and kept the others. It is false, but false is still one of the two values.
byKey.dropped-unknown: You left out row 8. Nobody knows yet whether it is true, but it must be one or the other.
byKey.took-open: You kept row 7. Its truth depends on $x$, which nobody has given, so it cannot be marked yet.
byKey.r1: You kept row 2. It is a question: it asks, it does not claim.
byKey.r3: You kept row 4. It is an order to do something, so it is neither true nor false.
byKey.r4: You kept row 5. “Best” has no agreed test, so it is an opinion, not a claim anyone can check.
byKey.r6: You kept row 7. Its truth depends on $x$, which nobody has given, so it cannot be marked yet.
byKey.r2: You left out row 3. It is false, since $91 = 7 \times 13$, but a false sentence can still be marked.
byKey.r7: You left out row 8. Nobody knows yet whether it is true, but it must be one or the other.

explain.text: Rows 1, 3, 6 and 8 each make a claim that is either true or false. A question, an order and an opinion make no such claim. Row 7 waits on a value for $x$.

screens.title: A statement
screens.prose: The sentences you kept have a name. A **statement** is a sentence that is either true or false, but not both. Its **truth value** is T or F.

rows: The FTSE 100 is the best index
Every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes

screens.question: Why is “The FTSE 100 is the best index” not a statement?

options.text: “Best” has no agreed test, so nobody can mark it true or false
It is false, because other indices beat it
options.why: You ruled it out for being false. A false sentence would still be a statement; this one cannot be marked at all.

options.text: It is written in words, not symbols
options.why: You ruled it out for using words. Row 1, “7 is prime”, is in words and is a statement.

options.text: Markets change, so it is true some days and false on others
options.why: You gave it a truth value that moves. It has none on any day, because “best” is never pinned down.

hints.text: What would you need in order to check the sentence?
Best by return, by size, or by cost? The sentence does not say.
With no agreed test for “best”, it is an opinion. It is neither true nor false.

feedback.correct: Right. “Best” is a matter of taste until someone says how it is measured.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what test would settle the sentence.

byKey.false: You ruled it out for being false. False sentences are statements too; this one cannot be marked at all.

explain.text: A statement needs a claim that can be checked. “Best” could mean highest return, largest size or lowest cost. Until one is chosen, the sentence has no truth value.

screens.title: Is 91 prime?
screens.prose: Row 3 says 91 is prime. A prime is a whole number above 1 whose only whole-number divisors are 1 and itself. Test the small primes in turn.
screens.question: What is $91 \div 7$?

hints.text: Count up in sevens: 70, 77, 84, ...
$7 \times 10 = 70$, and 21 more is $7 \times 3$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the whole number that 7 multiplies to give 91.

explain.text: $91 = 7 \times 13$, so 91 has a divisor other than 1 and itself. “91 is prime” is a statement with truth value F.

screens.title: A power of two
screens.prose: Row 6 says $2^{10} > 1000$. Doubling from 2 ten times builds $2^{10}$ one step at a time.
screens.question: What is the truth value of $2^{10} > 1000$?

options.why: You multiplied 2 by 10. A power multiplies ten 2s together.
You worked out $10^2$. Here the 2 is the base and 10 is the power.

options.text: Neither: it uses symbols, so it is not a statement
options.why: You ruled it out for its symbols. $>$ is shorthand for the words “is greater than”.

hints.text: Each row of the table doubles the one before.
$2^9 = 512$. One more doubling gives $2^{10}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Double 512 once more and compare with 1000.

byKey.twenty: You multiplied 2 by 10. $2^{10}$ is ten 2s multiplied: 1024.
byKey.hundred: You worked out $10^2 = 100$. The power is 10 here, so $2^{10} = 1024$.

explain.text: Doubling 512 gives $2^{10} = 1024$. Since $1024 > 1000$, the statement is true.

screens.title: Pin the words down
screens.prose: A risk report gives yesterday's result for one desk. Someone writes “yesterday was a large loss”.
screens.question: Which version is a statement we can check against the report?

options.text: Yesterday's loss was more than £1,000
Yesterday's loss was large
options.why: You kept “large”. Large to one desk is small to another, so it has no truth value until a threshold is given.

options.text: Was yesterday's loss large?
options.why: You picked a question. A question asks; it does not claim anything.

options.text: Keep losses small
options.why: You picked an instruction. An instruction is obeyed or not, but it is not true or false.

hints.text: Which sentence gives a test you could run on the number in the report?
Only one option names an amount.
“More than £1,000” can be checked against £1,240. It is true.

feedback.correct: Right. With a threshold of £1,000 the sentence is a statement, and it is true.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the sentence that gives an exact test.

byKey.large: You kept “large”. Without a threshold it cannot be checked, so it is not yet a statement.

explain.text: “Large” is vague, so “yesterday's loss was large” has no truth value. “More than £1,000” gives a test. The loss was £1,240, so the statement is true.

screens.title: Waiting for $x$
screens.prose: Row 7 was $x + 2 = 5$. It is an **open sentence**: its truth depends on $x$. Each dot is a value $x$ could take.
screens.question: Tap every value of $x$ that makes $x + 2 = 5$ a true statement.

hints.text: Try one dot: put its number in place of $x$ and add 2.
Which number plus 2 makes 5?
$3 + 2 = 5$. Every other dot gives a false statement.

feedback.correct: Only $x = 3$. Every other value turns the sentence into a false statement.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put each value in place of $x$ and check whether the sum is 5.

byKey.five: You tapped 5, the right-hand side. $5 + 2 = 7$, not 5.
byKey.two: You tapped 2, the number being added. $2 + 2 = 4$, not 5.

explain.text: Once $x$ is given, $x + 2 = 5$ becomes a statement. It is true for $x = 3$ and false for every other value. The set of values that make it true, here just $\{3\}$, is its **truth set**.

screens.title: A false statement
screens.prose: Look again at row 3, “91 is prime”. We showed that $91 = 7 \times 13$.

rows: The FTSE 100 is the best index
Every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes

screens.question: Is “91 is prime” a statement?

options.text: Yes. It is a statement, and its truth value is F
No. It is false, so it is not a statement
options.why: You ruled it out because it is false. A statement only has to be true or false, and this one is false.

options.text: No. We had to work it out, so it is not a statement
options.why: You ruled it out because checking took work. A statement needs a truth value, not an easy one.

options.text: It is both true and false, since 91 looks prime
options.why: Looking prime is not being prime. It is false, and a statement is never both.

hints.text: What does a sentence need in order to be a statement?
A statement is true or false. Which one is row 3?
Row 3 is false. Being false is one of the two allowed values.

feedback.correct: Yes. A false statement is still a statement.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall what a statement needs: one of the two truth values.

byKey.false-not: You ruled it out because it is false. False is one of the two values a statement can have, so it stays a statement.

explain.text: A statement must be true or false, and “91 is prime” is false. Being false does not stop it being a statement. Most claims we disprove later are false statements.

canvas.caption: “91 is prime”: a statement with value F

screens.title: Nobody knows yet
screens.prose: Row 8 is Goldbach's conjecture from 1742. Computers have checked it for every even number up to $4 \times 10^{18}$. Nobody has proved it or found a case where it fails.

rows: The FTSE 100 is the best index
Every even number greater than 2 is the sum of two primes

screens.question: Is row 8 a statement?

options.text: Yes. It is true or false, even though nobody knows which
No. A statement must have a known truth value
options.why: You asked for a known value. A statement needs a value, whether or not anyone has found it.

options.text: No. It talks about infinitely many numbers
options.why: You ruled it out for covering infinitely many numbers. “Every even number is a whole number” does too, and it is true.

options.text: Yes, and it is true, since it has been checked so far
options.why: You took checked cases as proof. A single even number beyond the checks could still fail.

hints.text: Does the sentence make a definite claim?
Either every even number above 2 is a sum of two primes, or some even number is not.
One of those must hold, so the sentence has a value. We just do not know it.

feedback.correct: Yes. It has a truth value; we just do not know it yet.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the claim is definite, not whether it is settled.

byKey.checked: You took checked cases as proof. Checking is evidence, and one even number beyond $4 \times 10^{18}$ could still fail.

explain.text: The sentence makes a definite claim about every even number above 2. So it is either true or false, which makes it a statement. Checking many cases is evidence, not proof.

screens.title: The rule
screens.prose:
You kept a sentence when it had to be one of two values:

$$\text{statement} = \text{a sentence that is T or F, not both}$$

Questions, orders and opinions are not statements. An open sentence becomes one once its letter is given a value.
screens.question: Which of these is a statement?

options.why: You picked the open sentence. With no value for $x$ it is not yet true or false.

options.text: Sell 100 shares at the open
options.why: You picked an order. It can be carried out, but it is not true or false.

options.text: Value investing is the smartest style
options.why: You picked an opinion. “Smartest” has no agreed test.

feedback.correct: Right. With $x = 4$ it reads $4 + 2 = 5$: a false statement.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look for the sentence that is already true or false.

byKey.open: You picked the open sentence. It becomes a statement only once $x$ is given.

explain.text: Giving $x$ the value 4 turns the open sentence into $4 + 2 = 5$. That is false, so it is a statement with value F.

screens.title: A limit a system can check
screens.prose: A risk system checks each desk's limits at the close. A limit is only useful if the system can mark it true or false from the numbers it holds.
screens.question: Which limits could the system enforce? Select all that apply.

options.text: Today's loss is under £50,000
No position is more than 10% of the book at the close
The desk takes sensible risk
options.why: You kept “sensible”. No number in the report can mark it true or false.

options.text: Traders should avoid big bets
options.why: You kept an instruction with a vague word. “Big” has no threshold, and an instruction is not true or false.

hints.text: For each wording, ask what number the system would compare.
Two wordings name an exact threshold.
“Under £50,000” and “more than 10% of the book” can be checked at the close. The other two cannot.

feedback.correct: Right. The two limits with exact thresholds are statements the system can check.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep a wording only if the numbers decide it.

byKey.sensible: You kept “sensible risk”. It names no threshold, so the system cannot mark it.
byKey.avoid: You kept “avoid big bets”. It is an instruction with no threshold.
byKey.loss: You left out the loss limit. Equities lost £32,400, which the system can compare with £50,000.
byKey.size: You left out the position limit. Rates holds £9.8m of £61m, about 16%, which the system can compare with 10%.

explain.text: A limit must be a statement the numbers can decide. Both desks pass the loss limit. Rates fails the position limit, since £9.8m is about 16% of £61m.

ideas: A statement is a sentence that is either true or false, not both. Questions, orders and opinions are not statements.
A false sentence is still a statement, and so is one whose truth value nobody knows yet.
An open sentence such as $x + 2 = 5$ becomes a statement once $x$ has a value. Its truth set holds the values that make it true.

formula.name: Statement
formula.tex: \text{a sentence that is } \mathrm{T} \text{ or } \mathrm{F}\text{, not both}
formula.note: Vague words must be pinned down first: “a loss of more than £1,000”, not “a large loss”.

summary.trap: “91 is prime” is false, and that makes it a false statement, not a non-statement.

quiz.prose: The open sentence $x > 3$ has the truth set drawn below: every number to the right of 3, with 3 itself left out.

4 is bigger than 3, so $4 > 3$ is true.

quiz.prose: About real numbers, $0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3$ is true. Yet in Python, `0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` gives `False`.
quiz.question: What explains the difference?

options.text: Python rounds 0.1 and 0.2, so it compares different numbers
The maths statement is really false
options.why: You trusted the code over the arithmetic. One tenth plus two tenths is exactly three tenths.

options.text: Neither is a statement, since they disagree
options.why: You ruled both out. Each one is definite; they are about different numbers.

options.text: The sentence is both true and false
options.why: A statement is never both. The two sentences are about different numbers.

feedback.correct: Right. Python's floats are rounded, so it compares two slightly different numbers.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether the code is about exactly 0.1 and 0.2.

explain.text: Python stores 0.1 and 0.2 in binary, rounded, so their sum is `0.30000000000000004`. The code tests that number against a rounded 0.3, which is a different statement.
